title: He knows your pain
hookLine: the Lord knows every heart's pain (Sukhmani 15)

lines: RATE YOUR PAIN, ONE TO TEN.
IT DOESN'T FEEL LIKE A NUMBER.
cards: The doctor asks you to rate your pain from one to ten, and you freeze. Is it a six? A seven?
It doesn't feel like a number. It feels like a color, or a weight, or a sound that won't stop. Some pain can't be explained to anybody.
You try, and the words come out too small, or too dramatic, and the person nods kindly and clearly doesn't get it. Today the fifteenth ashtpadi names the One who doesn't need the number.

teach.b: Yesterday's salok called God sarab kalaa bharpoor, brimful of every power. In the same breath it says birthaa jaananhaar. Jaananhaar: the one who knows.

Birthaa: the inner condition, especially its pain, what's going on in you that nobody can see. So: the knower of every heart's pain. Put the two halves together and they say something that matters a great deal.
Power without knowing would be frightening, a force that can do anything but doesn't notice you. Knowing without power would be sad, a friend who understands but can't help.
The salok holds both in one line: the One who can do anything already knows exactly what's wrong.
The ashtpadi's first stanza gives the picture a tender name: the mender of the broken, who joins what has snapped, like a carpenter fitting a cracked chair leg back together.
The same stanza says God carries the care of all beings in mind. Notice what this doesn't say. It doesn't say the pain isn't real, or that it's deserved, or that it'll be gone by tomorrow.
Gurbani is honest about suffering; the Gurus lived through plenty of it, and Guru Arjan himself, who wrote these words, was later tortured and killed. What it says is that the pain is known.

teach.h: NO NEED TO EXPLAIN IT WELL.
teach.b: You don't have to find the right number, or explain it well.
For many Sikhs, that's where prayer starts: not with getting the words right, but with remembering that the hurt is already known.

how: Sikhs reciting Sukhmani Sahib name God birthaa jaananhaar, the knower of every pain, in the fifteenth ashtpadi's salok, and many bring their troubles silently to the Guru in prayer and in the Ardas.

o: a birthday, the day a new life begins
a sin that must be confessed out loud
the heart's inner pain, unseen by others

games.q: he knows your pain — tap the pairs.

s: the salok says pain is unreal once God knows it
it says the pain is known, not that it isn't real.
the salok pairs God's full power with knowing every pain
sarab kalaa bharpoor and birthaa jaananhaar sit in one line.
in this teaching, you must describe your pain correctly for it to be known
the knowing is already there; no words are needed.

games.q: you're hurting and can't find words for it, even for yourself. what does the fifteenth ashtpadi offer?
o: it's already known by the knower of every pain.
keep it to yourself; nobody can know.
games.why: birthaa jaananhaar: the One who holds all power already knows the pain inside. no right number required.

practice: Let one hurt come to mind, big or small, a worry, an ache, a grief that won't settle, and without explaining or rating it, turn toward it and let it be seen, the way you'd hold a cut finger up to someone who loves you.
If you pray, you can offer it to Waheguru without words. If you don't, let it be fully known by you, for once, without hurrying away.

wordCard.voice: Birthaa, the heart's inner pain. The One full of every power also knows it, the mender of what's broken.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: birthaa, here the inner state or pain; the word can also mean 'in vain' elsewhere in Gurbani.

carryVoice: Your line: he knows. No number needed, and no need to explain it well. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Sukhmani Sahib, ashtpadi 15, salok and stanza 1 (Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 282)
